title: "Getting started"
---

```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
```

```{r setup}
library(sasonr)
```

## Run a SAS program

`sas_run()` takes SAS source code, runs it on the R engine and returns the
log, the listing and the WORK data sets.

```{r}
code <- "
data dm;
  input usubjid $ age sex $;
  datalines;
S01 45 M
S02 70 F
S03 .  F
;
run;

data adsl;
  set dm;
  length agegr1 $5;
  if missing(age) then agegr1 = 'Miss';
  else if age < 65 then agegr1 = '<65';
  else agegr1 = '>=65';
  put usubjid= age= agegr1=;
run;
"
res <- sas_run(code)
sas_log(res)
res$work$adsl
```

Missing values have SAS semantics (a missing numeric value is smaller than
any number), and character variables have a fixed length, here set by the
`LENGTH` statement.

## Translate a program into an R script

`sas_script()` writes the translation of a program as an R script that runs
after `library(sasonr)`. With `tidy = TRUE`, each vectorised DATA step becomes
a dplyr pipe on R data frames (the script loads dplyr and tidylog, so every
step reports what it did); steps that need sasonr's own runtime run in a short
session block.

```{r}
code2 <- "
data lab;
  input usubjid $ visit aval;
  datalines;
S01 1 10
S01 2 12
S02 1 20
S02 2 18
;
run;

data chg;
  set lab;
  by usubjid;
  retain base;
  if first.usubjid then base = aval;
  chg = aval - base;
run;
"
sas_script(sas_translate(code2), tidy = TRUE)
```

Without `tidy`, every SAS step becomes one call of a step verb on a session:
`sas_data_step()` holds the generated code of a DATA step and the SAS text it
came from, `sas_proc_sort()` and `sas_proc_means()` show the options the
program gave, and other steps keep their SAS text. This script gives the same
WORK data sets and the same log as `sas_run()`.

```{r}
code3 <- "
data adsl;
  input usubjid $ age;
  datalines;
S01 70
S02 41
;
run;
proc sort data=adsl out=bysubj; by descending age; run;
"
sas_script(sas_translate(code3))
```

`sas_script()` also takes the result of `sas_run()`: the script is then the
trace of that run, including the steps that macro code generated.

## Look at the code of one step

`sas_translate()` returns the generated R code step by step, for debugging.
Simple steps become vectorised `dplyr` pipelines; steps with cross-row state
such as `RETAIN`, `LAG` or `FIRST.`/`LAST.` use grouped vectorised code when
the result can be proven identical, and an explicit row loop otherwise. The
header of each step names its level and the reason.

```{r}
tr <- sas_translate(code2)
cat(tr$steps[[2]]$code)
sas_run(code2)$work$chg
```

## Macro language

Macro processing and step execution interleave: a step is run as soon as it
is complete, so values created with `CALL SYMPUTX` are
available to the macro code that follows.

```{r}
code3 <- "
%macro check(ds);
  data _null_;
    call symputx('n', 3);
  run;
  %if &n > 2 %then %put NOTE: &ds is large;
  %else %put NOTE: &ds is small;
%mend check;
%check(adsl)
"
sas_log(sas_run(code3), echo = FALSE)
```

`echo = FALSE` leaves the program lines out: the log shows only the
messages and the PUT output.

## Unsupported features fail loudly

sasonr never guesses. A feature it does not support stops the program with
a classed condition that carries the SAS line number.

```{r, error = TRUE}
sas_run("data a; x = 1; run; proc report data=a; run;")
```

The same applies by default (`sasonr.strict = TRUE`) to functions, formats
and informats whose status in the feature registry is `approximate`
(the last bits of numeric results may not be exact, for example in the
probability functions) or `unsupported`: they stop with a `sasonr_strict_error`
condition (see `?sasonr_strict`).

```{r, error = TRUE}
sas_run("data a; p = probnorm(1.96); run;")
```

To run them anyway, with a warning of class `sasonr_strict_warning`, turn
strict mode off:

```{r}
old <- options(sasonr.strict = FALSE)
res <- suppressWarnings(sas_run("data a; p = probnorm(1.96); run;"))
res$work$a$p
options(old)
```
